summary: HORIZON is an educational project made of two connected browser games that teach children aged 7 to 12 how a Mars base really works. In Mission Jezero, a 3D globe built from real NASA images (Viking, MRO CTX and HiRISE) leads players to Jezero Crater, where they build a base and decide each sol how to split power between air, shielding and science. In Arcadia Colony, they become the commander on the surface: going out on EVA, building with Martian resources, and protecting the crew from solar storms, marsquakes and dust. The project addresses the challenge by covering life support, radiation protection, power, food, water and communication delay, with NASA data driving every decision: live DONKI space weather triggers solar alerts, and real results from Curiosity, Perseverance’s MOXIE, InSight and Phoenix shape the rules. It matters because space content for kids is often abstract or too technical, showing results but never the reasoning behind them. Here, every choice has a real cost explained on screen, so children learn by trying, failing and thinking like engineers.
details: HORIZON is an educational browser game for children aged 7 to 12, made of two connected parts. In Mission Jezero, a 3D globe built from real NASA images (Viking MDIM 2.1, MRO CTX and HiRISE, via NASA Mars Trek) takes the player down to Jezero Crater. There they found a base and act as mission control, splitting each sol’s power between air, shielding and science after seeing a forecast. In Arcadia Colony, they become the commander on the surface: they go out on EVA through the airlock, build with Martian resources such as regolith, ice and iron, manage food, water and oxygen, and protect the crew from solar storms, marsquakes, meteorites and dust. Live space weather from NASA’s DONKI decides when solar alerts happen, which real event they come from and when the cloud reaches Mars. HORIZON turns abstract space science into decisions children can feel: every choice has a real cost explained on screen, and a “go back 1 sol” button lets a class compare strategies. It runs in any browser with no download or sign-up, so it works on ordinary school computers, tablets and phones. Our intended impact is to teach the reasoning behind space missions, not just their results, so children learn that saving power today can cost oxygen tomorrow and come to see engineering and NASA data as tools for making decisions. We built it with HTML, CSS and JavaScript, Three.js (WebGL) for 3D, TypeScript, React and Vite on the Lovable platform, and Node.js for automated tests. It uses the NASA DONKI API and NASA Mars Trek image tiles, CC0 assets from Kenney and Poly Haven, and is hosted on Netlify. The code, texts and 3D visuals were generated with generative AI (Anthropic Claude and Lovable AI) under the team’s direction, as declared in AI-USE.md. The creative side lies in two linked views of one mission, in solar alerts that can be false alarms (the real dilemma of a flight director), in building the colony from Martian materials, and in natural disasters that come from our own Java disaster simulator. We designed it for its age group, with simple language, a glossary, a guide character and a Cadet Mode with only three resources. We kept every number scientifically honest and cited its source, made sure it runs on low-end devices and is fun to replay, respected NASA’s brand rules by crediting without logos, and disclosed our AI use openly.
